2. Command Execution:

   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text

   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 600000ms / 10 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

12	
13	Build `wordstat`, a small Python 3.11+ command-line utility invoked from the repository root as `python -m wordstat [--json] [--top N] FILE`. It reads exactly one UTF-8 file, optionally with a leading BOM, computes counts and the most frequent tokens, then emits deterministic text or JSON output. The implementation uses only the Python standard library; pytest is permitted for tests only. The repository-root `contract.md` is the authoritative source for every required behavior and takes precedence over this supporting specification and the brief.
14	
15	## 2. Problem Statement
16	
17	### Current State
18	
19	The repository currently contains the feature brief and interface contract but no application package, tests, dependency manifest, or established project-specific code conventions. The brief requests a small standalone tool and pytest tests (`brief.md:1`).
20	
21	### Impact of Inaction
22	
23	Without the implementation, users cannot run the requested module, and there is no automated evidence for the specified cross-platform output, counting rules, or failure behavior.
24	
25	## 3. Goals & Non-Goals
26	
27	### Goals
28	
29	- Provide a working `python -m wordstat ...` entry point from the repository root.
30	- Meet all functional, formatting, encoding, determinism, and exit-code requirements in root `contract.md` R1–R6 and its interface contract.
31	- Include pytest tests that exercise the real CLI and the required edge cases.
32	- Keep application runtime dependencies to the Python 3.11+ standard library.
33	
34	### Non-Goals
35	
36	- Reading from stdin, processing multiple files, recursion, or directory traversal.
37	- Installation/packaging, a public library API, configurable tokenization, stemming, or locale-sensitive behavior.
38	- Changing the authoritative contract to simplify implementation or tests.
39	
40	## 4. Architecture
41	
42	- Add a flat-layout `wordstat/` package at the repository root. `wordstat/__main__.py` supplies the module entry point; small pure helpers may be placed alongside it if that improves clarity, but no additional architecture is required.
43	- Add pytest coverage under `tests/`. Tests should invoke the current interpreter with `-m wordstat` from the repository root using subprocesses where CLI behavior, raw output bytes, or exit codes matter.
44	- Use only standard-library modules in production code (for example, `argparse`, `json`, `re`, and `collections`). No runtime package installation or external services are needed.
45	- Construct output only after the complete input has been read and validated, so the specified file and decoding errors leave stdout empty.
46	
47	## 5. Detailed Design
48	
49	### Command and argument parsing
50	
51	- Support exactly `python -m wordstat [--json] [--top N] FILE`; accept one positional file path and do not consume stdin.
52	- Use `argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="wordstat")`.
53	- `--json` selects JSON output; absent it, emit the text format.
54	- `--top` defaults to 3 and must parse as an integer >= 1. Invalid, missing, or unknown arguments use argparse's default usage-error behavior and exit 2.
55	- The contract does not narrow the lexical forms accepted by Python's integer conversion. Use normal `int` parsing plus a positive-value check rather than imposing an undocumented digit-only grammar.
56	
57	### Input and counts
58	
59	- Read the specified file once as UTF-8 with optional leading BOM removed (`utf-8-sig`) and strict decoding. Never read stdin.
60	- Preserve decoded newline code points while reading (for example, text-mode `newline=""`) so `chars` is the length of decoded text with only the optional initial BOM removed; do not introduce universal-newline normalization. This resolves the contract's input-newline ambiguity in favor of the literal `len(text)` requirement. `splitlines()` still determines the line count.
61	- Compute `lines = len(text.splitlines())`.
62	- Compute `tokens` as all matches of `[a-z0-9]+` in `text.lower()`; do not substitute a Unicode word-boundary definition, `casefold()`, or locale-aware processing.
63	- Compute `words = len(tokens)` and `chars = len(text)` (Python string code points).
64	- Count tokens and select at most N by descending frequency, then ascending token text. Do not rely on `Counter.most_common()` encounter order for ties. If fewer than N distinct tokens exist, return all of them.
65	
66	### Output
67	
68	- Reconfigure stdout to `encoding="utf-8", newline="\n"` before writing output. Do not use locale-dependent formatting.
69	- Text output is exactly four lines, each terminated by `\n`:
70	  - `lines: <lines>`
71	  - `words: <words>`
72	  - `chars: <chars>`
73	  - `top: <word>=<count> <word>=<count> ...`
74	- When there are no tokens, the fourth line is exactly `top:` followed by `\n`, with no trailing space.
75	- JSON output is one `json.dumps(obj)` line with default separators followed by `\n`. Construct keys in the order `lines`, `words`, `chars`, `top`; each top entry has keys `word`, then `count`. Do not add indentation or sort keys.
76	- The contract explicitly requires stdout's encoding and newline configuration. Stderr diagnostics must satisfy the specified message and exit behavior; the contract does not separately define stderr byte encoding.
77	
78	### Errors and exit status
79	
80	- For missing, directory, or unreadable paths, and for other expected file-system `OSError`s during open/read, emit one line to stderr with prefix `wordstat: error: ` followed by the FILE argument exactly as supplied and `: cannot read file`; exit 3.
81	- For invalid UTF-8, emit one line with the same prefix followed by the original FILE argument and `: not valid UTF-8`; exit 3.
82	- File access exceptions can occur during reading as well as opening. Handle `UnicodeDecodeError` separately from `OSError` so invalid data receives the required message.
83	- Usage errors exit 2 and retain argparse's default usage output. The specific usage-error contract requires that the last stderr line match `^wordstat: error: `; this takes precedence over the general one-line error wording for those cases.
84	- Return 0 for success, including an empty file. Exit 1 remains reserved for unexpected internal errors. Specified bad-input cases must not produce a traceback.

86	## 6. Cost Estimates

88	No external services, paid APIs, or runtime packages are required. The only ongoing cost is local execution and maintenance of a small Python package and pytest suite.

96	
97	- **Newline translation changes character counts:** preserve CR, LF, and CRLF while decoding; test raw CRLF and CR inputs and assert both `chars` and `lines`.
98	- **Tokenization or tie-order drift:** encode the precise lower-then-ASCII-regex formula and frequency/lexical sorting in focused tests.
99	- **Platform-dependent output:** configure stdout encoding/newlines explicitly and assert subprocess output bytes rather than normalized text.
100	- **Partial output on bad input:** finish file read and validation before writing any stdout; test stdout is empty on all specified read/decode failures.
101	- **Unportable permission tests:** cover portable missing-path and directory failures; test permission failure only where the environment can reliably produce it, while mapping `OSError` generally.
102	- **Argparse behavior conflicts with generic one-line wording:** preserve the more specific required argparse default behavior and assert the required status and final stderr-line prefix.

104	## 9. Acceptance Criteria
105	
106	Acceptance is measured against the root `contract.md` and requires all of the following:
107	
108	1. `python -m wordstat --help` exits 0 (R1).
109	2. The command reads exactly one supplied file as UTF-8 with an optional BOM, never reads stdin, and uses the required Python 3.11+ standard-library-only application stack (R2).

1	# wordstat: Interface Contract
2	
3	## Constraints
4	
5	- **Stack:** Python >=3.11, standard library only; pytest for tests only.
6	- **Package location:** `wordstat/` at repo root (flat layout, no `src/`).
7	- **Entry point:** `python -m wordstat ...` run from repo root.
8	
9	## Functional requirements
10	
11	- **R1** `python -m wordstat --help` exits 0.
12	- **R2** `python -m wordstat [--json] [--top N] FILE` reads exactly one file, decoded as UTF-8 with an optional BOM (`utf-8-sig`). stdin is never read.
13	- **R3** Counts, computed on the decoded text:
14	  - `lines` = `len(text.splitlines())`
15	  - `words` = number of matches of `[a-z0-9]+` in `text.lower()`
16	  - `chars` = `len(text)` (code points, BOM excluded)
17	- **R4** `top` lists the `N` most frequent words (same tokens as R3), ordered by count descending, then word ascending. `--top` defaults to 3. Fewer than `N` distinct words lists all of them.
18	- **R5** Default output is the text format; `--json` selects the JSON format.
19	- **R6** Output is deterministic: UTF-8, `\n` line endings, no locale use. stdout is reconfigured to `encoding="utf-8", newline="\n"`.
20	
21	## Interface contract
22	
23	### Command
24	
25	```
26	python -m wordstat [--json] [--top N] FILE
27	```
28	
29	- argparse `prog` is `wordstat`.
30	- `--top` must be an integer >= 1, else usage error.
31	
32	### Text format
33	
34	Exactly four lines, each ending in `\n`:
35	
36	```
37	lines: <lines>
38	words: <words>
39	chars: <chars>
40	top: <word>=<count> <word>=<count> ...
41	```
42	
43	With no words, the last line is `top:` with no trailing space.
44	
45	### JSON format
46	
47	One line: the result of `json.dumps(obj)` with default separators, followed by `\n`, where `obj` has keys in this order:
48	
49	```
50	{"lines": <int>, "words": <int>, "chars": <int>, "top": [{"word": <str>, "count": <int>}, ...]}
51	```
52	
53	### Exit codes and errors
54	
55	Errors print one line to stderr, prefix `wordstat: error: `, and leave stdout empty. `<path>` is the FILE argument exactly as given.
56	
57	| Condition | Exit | stderr (after prefix) |
58	|---|---|---|
59	| File missing, a directory, or unreadable | 3 | `<path>: cannot read file` |
60	| Not valid UTF-8 | 3 | `<path>: not valid UTF-8` |
61	| Usage error (missing FILE, unknown flag, bad `--top`) | 2 | argparse default; the last stderr line must match `^wordstat: error: ` |
62	
63	Exit 0 on success, including an empty file. Exit 1 is reserved for unexpected internal errors.
64	
65	## Example
66	
67	`sample.txt` (UTF-8, `\n` endings):
68	
69	```
70	The cat sat.
71	The cat ran!
72	A dog.
73	```
74	
75	`python -m wordstat sample.txt` → exit 0, stdout:
76	
77	```
78	lines: 3
79	words: 8
80	chars: 33
81	top: cat=2 the=2 a=1
82	```
83	
84	`python -m wordstat --json --top 2 sample.txt` → exit 0, stdout:
85	
86	```
87	{"lines": 3, "words": 8, "chars": 33, "top": [{"word": "cat", "count": 2}, {"word": "the", "count": 2}]}
88	```

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 600000ms / 10 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice.

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 600000 ms, max 7200000 ms).

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

content.content:
1	Build `wordstat`, a tiny Python command-line tool that reads one UTF-8 text file and prints its line, word and character counts plus its most frequent words. It must run as `python -m wordstat FILE` from the repository root using only the Python 3.11+ standard library. Output is a short text summary by default or one line of JSON with `--json`; `--top N` sets how many frequent words to show. Output must be byte-for-byte deterministic on Windows, macOS and Linux. Bad input must fail cleanly with a clear message on stderr and a specific exit code, never a traceback. The full interface contract is in `contract.md`; include pytest tests for your implementation.
2

1	# AGENTS.md — geeky-orchestration
2	
3	Guidance for **any** AI coding agent (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Cursor, Windsurf,
4	Copilot CLI, Gemini CLI, or an SDK/LangGraph orchestrator) working with this
5	plugin's plan → execute → track workflow. Claude Code reads this via `@AGENTS.md`;
6	most other CLI agents read `AGENTS.md` natively.
7	
8	## Eval operator readiness
9	
10	This section applies only to operators in the source checkout. Contestant exports deliberately omit `evals/`; exported contestants must follow the canonical authorization and exported skills without looking for these operator files or adding a new approval gate. For source-checkout C0 preparation, read [current readiness](evals/c0-readiness.md) and [lessons learned](evals/lessons-learned.md). Generate fresh offline inventory and verify its exact HEAD, source hashes and prompt hash before a separately authorized live action. Local inventory and mock success grant no launch or telemetry publication authority. Preserve historical evidence and scores. Record desired and observed model/effort by role, the authorization reference, attempt/recovery limits, reserve and existing qualification waiver. Once a particular contestant run is authorized, retain the end-to-end workflow permissions already granted by its canonical prompt.
11	
12	## The workflow
13	
14	1. **spec-research** — research and write `feature-specification.md`.
15	2. **geeky-plan** — create the frozen planning package.
16	3. **plan-review** — validate alignment, coverage, sequencing, and readiness.
17	4. **geeky-status** — read-only status and resumption orientation at any packet stage.
18	5. **geeky-implement** — execute Ready tasks with validation and review gates.
19	6. **impl-review** — review delivered code through three domain-specific lanes.
20	7. **archive** — move completed planning artifacts into the archive structure.
21	
22	Use **geeky-orchestrator** when the requested entry point is unclear or when one
23	agent should administer the lifecycle. It examines repository evidence read-only
24	and recommends a workflow before mutation. Clear, explicit requests route to the
25	best matching skill after prerequisite checks. Material ambiguity is clarified;
26	stages are not auto-chained without end-to-end authorization.
27	
28	Full procedures live in the portable Skills under `skills/<name>/SKILL.md`.
29	
30	## Workflow terminology
31	
32	Use these meanings across skills, briefs and reports. They describe the orchestration
33	domain; retain the target project's own domain language. Existing filenames, schema
34	fields and checkpoint markers remain unchanged.
35	
36	| Term | Meaning |
37	|---|---|
38	| Planning package | Specification, plan, task contracts and tracking artifacts for one approved outcome. "Packet" is an alias; planning folder is its location. |
39	| Workflow stage | A lifecycle activity such as planning, implementation or final implementation review. Numbered "phases" inside a skill are procedure steps, not implementation phases. |
40	| Implementation phase | A group of tasks whose combined requirements are reviewed before advancement. "Wave" means a scheduling group unless the plan explicitly equates it with a phase. |
41	| Task | A bounded unit with an ID, scope, dependencies, acceptance criteria (ACs) and required validation. |
42	| Requirement / AC / Definition of Done | Required outcome or constraint / observable condition for satisfying it / completion conditions for the task. Required tests supply evidence; they do not replace ACs. |
43	| Task contract | The frozen task body and applicable approved requirements. A task brief conveys that contract to a worker. |
44	| Validation | Checks of the work. Validation evidence records what ran or was observed, against which inputs, and the result; a PASS claim alone is not evidence. |
45	| Review | Judgment of evidence against an assigned scope. Task review checks ACs/tests; phase review decides readiness to advance; final implementation review uses `impl-review`. Plan review evaluates the planning package. |
46	| Acceptance | The decision that required outcomes and gates for the stated scope are satisfied. Task Done, phase READY TO ADVANCE and final review PASS have different scopes; none grants release or deployment approval. |
47	| Finding | An evidenced discrepancy. A blocking finding prevents the current contract from being met; an optional improvement is a follow-up. Severity labels retain their review-stage meanings, not an automatic cross-stage mapping. |
48	| Execution batch / review batch | Tasks dispatched together / tasks sharing a reviewer assignment. Each phase has one review batch, the phase review: members wait in In Review until it clears, and each keeps its own verdict. |
49	| Orchestrator / worker / reviewer | Coordinates and accepts work / performs a bounded assignment / evaluates it. `geeky-coder` is the implementation worker; PM describes a planning or phase-review perspective. |
50	
51	## The planning-folder contract
52	
53	**Frozen** (never edit mid-run — they are the contract between plan and implement):
54	`implementation-plan.md`, `feature-specification.md`, `draft.md`, `references.md`,
55	and every `tasks/Tx-*.md` body. If the plan is genuinely wrong, surface it via the
56	kanban **Blocked** lane + `handoff.md` instead of editing the contract.
57	
58	**Mutable** (update continuously during implement):
59	`kanban.md` (single source of truth for lane status), `handoff.md` (running log),
60	and `tasks/Tx-*.notes.md` (per-task notes — these are writable, unlike the task bodies).
61	
62	Record a consequence for another task in that task's notes and in `handoff.md`.
63	
64	## Deterministic quality gates (run these — don't self-report)
65	
66	These replace "I updated the board / the task is done" with fail-stop checks.
67	Every gate: **arguments in, exit 0 = pass / exit 1 = fail, summary on stdout**,
68	optional `--json` / `-Json`. Each ships paired Python + PowerShell with identical
69	behavior. `geeky.manifest.json` is the machine-readable index of the same list.
70	
71	Paths below are relative to this plugin root (`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` in Claude Code).
72	Use `python3` where `python` is not on PATH; use `pwsh` (PowerShell 7+) for the `.ps1`.
73	
74	| Gate | When | Python | PowerShell |
75	|---|---|---|---|
76	| Planning-folder valid | start of implement/status | `python scripts/validate-planning-folder.py --path "<folder>"` | `pwsh -File scripts/validate-planning-folder.ps1 -Path "<folder>"` |
77	| Task-file schema | end of plan; start of implement | `python scripts/validate-task-schema.py --path "<folder>"` | `pwsh -File scripts/validate-task-schema.ps1 -Path "<folder>"` |
78	| Kanban integrity | after every lane move | `python scripts/validate-kanban.py --path "<folder>"` | `pwsh -File scripts/validate-kanban.ps1 -Path "<folder>"` |
79	| Definition of Done | in the Done step: move the task to Done, run this gate in the same step, move it back out on failure (D92) | `python scripts/check-dod.py --path "<folder>" --task <ID>` | `pwsh -File scripts/check-dod.ps1 -Path "<folder>" -Task <ID>` |
80	| Commit message | before each commit | `python scripts/check-commit.py --message "<msg>"` (or `<FILE>`) | `pwsh -File scripts/check-commit.ps1 -Message "<msg>"` (or `<FILE>`) |
81	
82	**Feedback loop:** when a gate exits non-zero, read its output, fix the artifact,
83	and re-run the same gate until it exits 0 before proceeding.
84	
85	## How each agent type runs the gates
86	
87	- **Claude Code:** the frozen-artifact guard fires automatically via
88	  `hooks/hooks.json` (PreToolUse). Run the validators above as explicit steps.
89	- **Other CLI agents (Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, Copilot, Gemini):** add an
90	  equivalent pre-edit/stop hook in your tool's config pointing at
91	  `hooks/guard-planning-contract.{py,ps1}` (it reads tool-call JSON on stdin,
92	  `--mode block` denies via JSON / exit 2). Invoke the validators as shell steps.
93	- **SDK / graph orchestrators (OpenAI Agents SDK, LangGraph):** call any validator
94	  with `subprocess.run([...])` inside a guardrail / node; raise a tripwire or
95	  `interrupt()` on a non-zero exit.
96	- **Any MCP-capable agent:** a bundled stdio MCP server (`geeky_mcp`, see `mcp/server.py`,
97	  registered in `.mcp.json`) exposes the gates as tools — `geeky_validate_planning_folder`,
